::: {#sol-shift-augment}

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
def random_shift(images, generator):
    # Move each image by its own random (rows, cols), each -1, 0 or 1.
    moves = torch.randint(-1, 2, (len(images), 2), generator=generator)
    out = images.clone()
    for rows in [-1, 0, 1]:
        for cols in [-1, 0, 1]:
            chosen = (moves[:, 0] == rows) & (moves[:, 1] == cols)
            out[chosen] = shift_images(images[chosen], rows, cols)
    return out


shift_net = make_net()
shift_history, shift_best_state = fit(shift_net, transform=random_shift)
shift_stopped = make_net()
_ = shift_stopped.load_state_dict(shift_best_state)
acc_shift = accuracy(shift_stopped, x_test, y_test)
print(acc_shift, acc_stopped)
```

The network trained on shifted images classifies `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * py$acc_shift)`% of the test images correctly at its best [epoch](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/gradient-descent.html#def-epoch),
against `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * py$acc_stopped)`% without shifts.
So the answer is `r if (py$acc_shift > py$acc_stopped) "yes" else "no"`.
Each pixel here counts the ink in a 4-by-4 block of a 32-by-32 bitmap [@alpaydin1998optdigits],
so a one-pixel shift moves the digit by 4 pixels of the original bitmap.
The test images are not shifted,
so a shifted training image is unlike the images the network is tested on.
A transformation for [data augmentation](#def-data-augmentation) should make inputs like the ones the network will see.

:::
